prompt: My friend just told me they lost their j
output:
A few traps worth avoiding:
- "It's for the best" or "everything happens for a reason." Even if you believe it, it lands like you're dismissing their grief before it's been felt.
- "At least..." comparisons. "At least it's not a layoff of thousands" or "at least you have savings" both tell them how grateful they should be instead of letting them be upset.
- "I know exactly how you feel." You don't, unless you've lived through this specific loss. "I can't imagine how hard this is" is closer to true.
- Laughter as a shield. Some people crack a joke to keep the mood light, and if the friend wanted lightness they'd have said it lightly themselves.
If they're the type who hates being pitied, just change the subject after the first sentence and be normal. "That sucks. Anyway, you said you were trying that new ramen place?" Normalcy is a real gift. It says: you are still my friend, your job isn't your whole identity to me.

When they tell you, keep it small and stay with them in it. You don't need the perfect sentence; you need to not panic or rush to fix things. "Oh no. Are you okay?" is a fine opener. "That sucks" is fine too. They've already processed what happened, they're not waiting for you to explain it back to them. What they're quietly watching for is whether your friendship survives the result, and the best answer to that is calm and plain.
The days after matter more than the first text. If they go quiet, don't push, but don't disappear either. "No need to reply, just checking in. I'm around whenever you want company." That keeps the door open without making them perform grief or gratitude on demand. When you do see them, make it normal. Bring food, suggest a walk, let them cry or laugh or talk about anything else. The message underneath the words is the one that lands: the result didn't change you.

prompt: My friend told me they're scared about a
output:
You don't need the perfect sentence. When someone tells you they're scared about a diagnosis, most of what they need isn't wisdom, it's to feel like you're not going to make them feel foolish or alone for being scared.
"I don't know what to say, and I hate that, but I'm glad you told me." This is honest, and honesty is usually better than performance. People are braced for a reaction, and you being visibly shaken too, in a steady way, tells them they don't have to carry it neatly.
Things to steer away from, even with good intentions:
Reframing, "everything happens for a reason," "this will make you stronger." Avoid "at least" sentences entirely.
Reflexive fixing, researching their condition, finding specialists, listing treatment options. Unless they ask, this usually lands as panic-mirroring, like you're trying to solve them. If they want information, they'll ask.
Making it about you, your own health scares, your cousin's story. One line of empathy is fine; a story is not.

I knew her face the way you know a word you've been reading all day. Twelve years hadn't changed her jaw. It had changed her eyes, made them flatter, more like a person doing math.
"Hi," she said. "You look like you've aged better than I expected."
The kettle was already on. I wanted to be angry about that, about the reflex of hospitality that fired in me before I could decide whether she was a person or a weather event, but I only said, "It's cold."
"It is." She stood in the doorway with a manila envelope under her arm, soft and worn at the edges, and she looked past me at the kitchen, the lamp, the radiator ticking its little argument with the window. "You're still here."
I moved aside to let her in, which was a mistake I recognized while it was happening. She came across the threshold and stood in the middle of the room like someone checking whether the floor would hold her.
"Good." She sat at the table with the envelope flat in front of her, spine down, like a closed book she'd brought from a library. She didn't touch it. She folded her hands on top of it. "I called the number on your listing. The county records office. Took three weeks and a fee and a good deal of typing my mother's name."
"Your mother's name," I repeated.
The kettle clicked off in the corner, which felt like it was happening to someone else. I filled the cup I'd poured for her twelve years ago, the mug with the chip on the handle, because I'd never been able to throw it out and couldn't figure out whether that was weakness or cowardice.
"Sit down," I said again, and this time I meant it.
She sat. I set the mug in front of her and stayed standing, hands on the counter, because my legs had started to do the thing where they want to leave the room entirely.
"You told me," Mara said, and her voice was careful, leveled, the tone of someone reading aloud from a document, "that Dad was driving that night. That he'd been drinking. That Mom was crying the whole way and screaming at him to stop, and he kept going." She looked up. "You said he was trying to leave us. That he'd packed his bags to take the car and go."
"I was twenty-two."
"I was nineteen. I was sitting in that kitchen in a bathrobe, and you were standing over me, and you said it like you were giving me news that had already been decided." She turned the mug in both hands, feeling its warmth without lifting it. "For twelve years I have believed that my mother died because my father was driving her somewhere she didn't want to go. That she died in the middle of a fight, being taken away from us."
The rain ticked on the porch roof. Somewhere down the street a dog barked at nothing, the way dogs do in November.
"She was driving," I said. "She'd been driving since we left town. Dad was asleep in the passenger seat. He'd been asleep for the last stretch, I don't know, twenty miles, thirty. She was talking to him the whole time, half-awake, half-frightened, and then the guardrail came out of the rain and that was it."
Mara's face didn't change. I watched her face not change, which was somehow worse than if she'd cried.
"And you kept it," she said.
"I kept it."
She sat there a long time. The mug cooled in her hands. Outside, the rain shifted to something heavier and the porch light swung its halo against the wet boards.
"I'm not going to hug you," Mara said.
"Understood."
She went to the desk by the window and opened the bottom drawer, because she knew it was there, had known since she was nine and twelve and fifteen, the way you know where a thing is hidden in a house you grew up in. She took out the key on its brass ring, the front-door key from the house on Weaver Street, the one she'd left behind the night she drove east with a duffel bag and no forwarding address.
She held it for a moment, then pocketed it with the envelope, both of them, her belongings, returned.
"Keep the mug," she said. "It was never yours to keep."
Then she walked out into the rain, and the screen door slammed its rusted hinge behind her, and I stood in the kitchen with the kettle ticking down and two mugs cooling on the counter, listening to her car pull away down the lane, its taillights shrinking to nothing at the end of the road.

output:
The 6:14 to the coast pulled away from the platform while I was still lacing my shoe.
The attendant looked at me with the professional sadness of someone who has seen this before.
"Forty minutes," she said. "To the next one."
Forty minutes. I had never once in my life been unable to leave a room faster.
I sat on the concrete bench under the flickering light and watched the rain arrive, the dark platform filling with the smell of diesel and wet wool. Somewhere behind me, a vending machine hummed and sold nothing.
There was a number I'd been postponing, a call I'd rehearsed and hung up from eleven times this week. Every time I'd had to go somewhere. Every time I'd been running.
I took out my phone. It rang, and rang, and then, at last, someone picked up.

- Form: a story (narrative, not just a scene fragment, though at 200 words it will be a vignette with some arc)
- Language: English

---Third night in a row I put Marcus's anorak in the dryer. The laundrette was mine except for a woman by the folding tables, her boiler broken since Tuesday, folding blankets under the fluorescents.
She watched me count coins twice. "It's the £150 one," she said. "The big one."
I nodded. Loaded the anorak, punched the coins in. The drum took it, settled it, began to turn.
Outside, the street stayed empty and cold. Inside, the machine clicked and spun and the detergent smell rose off everything, warm cotton, hot water, the smell of a factory.
"He's not coming back for it?" she asked.
"Marcus moved out in September."
"Then why wash it?"
I didn't have an answer ready. I watched the anorak tumble, green underside showing, torn hem flapping. "I don't know," I said. "I keep meaning to put it in the bin. Every night I keep meaning to."
She folded a blanket in thirds, neat as a hospital ward. "You can't bin something by accident either," she said. "You have to mean it twice."
The buzzer went. I opened the door, pulled the anorak out, and for the first time in three nights I didn't reload it. I folded it, sleeves in, the way Marcus did, and put it in the bag.
She was gone before I paid. Or maybe not, maybe she was still there, folding. The lights were still on.
